source_text: Talia quaedam de repromissionibus divinis credimus sentienda, cum intellegentiam nostram ad contemplationem aeterni illius et nullo fine elaudendi saeculi iaculamur atque ineffabilem eius laetitiam ae beatitudinem contemplamur. Verum quoniam in ecclesiastica praedicatione inest etiam de futuro ‚15 dei (iusto) iudicio fides, quae iudieii eredulitas provocat homines et suadet ad bene beateque vivendum et omni genere refugere peccatum, et per hoc sine dubio indieatur quod in nostra sit positum potestate vel laudabili nos vitae vel culpabili dedere: propterea necessarium reor pauca etiam de arbitrii nostri libertate disserere, eo quod non ignobiliter (20 haee quoque quaestio a quam plurimis agitetur. Ut autem facilius quid sit libertas arbitrii cognoscamus, quid sibi velit natura ipsius arbitrii voluntatisque requiramus. 2. Omnium quae moventur alia in semet ipsis causas motuum suorum gerunt, alia extrinsecus accipiunt: ut puta extrinsecus tantummodo moventur omnia, quae sine vita sunt, ut lapides vel ligna et quaeeumque huiusmodi sunt, quae solo habitu materiae suae vel corporum constant. Omittenda sane nune est illa quaestio, quae etiam illum motum putat esse, cum per corruptelam corpora dissolvuntur; nihil enim nunc haee ad propositum conducunt. Alia vero in semet ipsis habent movendi causam, ut animalia vel arbores et omnia, quae vel per naturalem vitam vel per animam constant; inter quae etiam metallorum venas deputari aliquibus visum est, sed et ignis sui motus esse putandus est, fortassis autem etiam fontes aquarum. Haec autem, quae in semet ipsis causam suorum motuum habent, quaedam dieunt ex se, quaedam ab se moveri; et ita dividunt quod ex se moveantur ea, quae vivunt quidem non tamen animantia sunt, a se autem moveantur animantia, cum eis fantasia, id est voluntas quaedam vel incitamentum, adfuerit, quae ea moveri ad aliquid vel incitari provocaverit. Denique etiam in quibusdam animalibus inest talis fantasia, id est voluntas vel sensus, qui ea natural quodam instinctu provocet et concitet ad ordinatos et conpositos motus; sieut videmus araneas facere, quae fantasia, id est voluntate quadam vel studio textrinae, ad opus texendi ordinatissime concitantur, sine dubio naturali quodam motu intentionem huiuscemodi operis provocante, nec tamen ultra alium ahquem sensum quam texendi naturale studium habere ipsum animal invenitur, sicut et apis fingendi favos ac mella, ut aiunt, aöria congre3. Rationabile vero animal cum habeat in se et hos naturales motus, habet tamen amplius ceteris animalibus etiam rationis vim, qua ludicare et discernere de motibus naturalibus possit et alios quidem reprobare et abicere alios vero probare atque suscipere, cuius rationis iudicio dirigi et gubernari hominis motus ad vitam probabilem possint. Unde consequens est ut, quoniam natura rationis huius, quae est in homine, habet in se vim dinoscendi boni vel mali, idque cum discreverit, inest ei facultas etiam eligendi quod probaverit, in eligendo quidem quod bonum est laudabilis, in sequendo vero quod turpe vel malum est iure culpabilis iudicetur. Illud sane nequaquam latere nos debet, quod in nonnullis mutis animalibus ordinatior quidam motus a ceteris animalibus invenitur, ut in sagacibus canibus vel bellatoribus equis, ita ut videantur aliquibus velut rationabili quodam sensu moveri; sed id non tam ratione quam incentivo quodam et naturah motu, pro huiuscemodi usibus largius indulto, fieri credendum est. Verum ut dieere eoeperamus, cum ita se habeat rationabile animal, nobis hominibus incidere quidem extrinsecus possunt aliqua et occurrere sive ad visum sive ad auditum vel ad alios sensus, quae nos concitent ac provocent ad bonos vel contrarios motus; quae utique quia extrinsecus incidunt, non est in nostra positum potestate ne incidant vel occurrant: iudieare vero et probare, qualiter uti debeamus his, quae incidunt, nullius alterius res est vel opus nisi rationis eius, quae est in nobis, id est nostri iudicii; euius rationis iudicio ineidentibus extrinsecus concitamentis abutimur ad id, quodcumque ipsa ratio probaverit, naturalibus motibus nostris nutu eius vel ad bona vel ad contraria guber4. Si vero quis dicat ea, quae extrinsecus incidunt motus nostros provocantia, talia esse, ut possibile non sit adversari eis, sive ad bonum nos sive ad malum concitantibus: in semet ipsum paulisper qui haee aestimat convertat animum et proprios diligentius introspieiat motus, nisi invenerit, cum alicuius desideri pulsat inlecebra, nihil prius geri quam animi accommodetur assensus et suggestioni pravae nutus mentis indulgeat; ita ut etiam verisimilibus quibusdam causis intra cordis nostri tribunalia velut iudici residenti ex utraque parte adhiberi videatur assertio, ut causis prius expositis gerundi sententia de rationis ludicio proferatur. Non enim, ut verbi gratia dixerim, hule, qui statuit continenter et easte vivere atque ab omni se muliebri contagio continere, si forte apparuerit mulier provocans eum et inliciens aliquid contra propositum gerere, causa ei (perfecta et absoluta) vel necessitas praevaricandi mulier extitit, cum possit utique statuti sui memor libidinis incitamenta refrenare et inritantis inlecebrae delectamenta austerioribus virtutis inerepationibus cohercere, ut omni luxuriae sensu fugato propositi firmitas et constantia perseveret. Denique si eruditioribus quibusque viris et in divinis insütutionibus roboratis huiuscemodi inritamenta provenerint, memores continuo sui, ea quae dudum meditati sunt et in quibus eruditi sunt in memoriam revocantes et sanctioris se doctrinae adminieulis munientes, respuunt ac refellunt omnem incitamenti inleeebram atque adversas concupiscentias insitae sibi rationis obiectione depellunt. 9.
pass_a_gloss: We believe certain things about divine promises are to be understood, when we direct our understanding to the contemplation of that eternal and endless praise and we contemplate its ineffable joy and beatitude. But since in ecclesiastical preaching there is also faith about the future judgment of God, which provokes the credibility of judgment and persuades men to live well and blessedly and to flee from every kind of sin, and through this it is undoubtedly indicated that it is in our power to give ourselves to a praiseworthy or culpable life: therefore I think it is necessary to discuss also a few things about the freedom of our will, because this question is also being discussed by very many people not ignobly. So that we may more easily know what the freedom of will is, we must investigate what the nature of will itself wants. Of all things that are moved, some have the causes of their movements within themselves, others receive them from outside: as, for example, all things that are without life are moved only from outside, such as stones or wood and whatever things of this kind are, which consist only in the habit of their matter or bodies. The question about whether even the movement of corruption, when bodies are dissolved, is a movement, is to be omitted now, because it does not contribute to the present purpose. But other things have the cause of movement within themselves, such as animals or trees and all things that consist either through natural life or through a soul; among which some people think that even the veins of metals and perhaps also the movement of fire and the sources of water are to be numbered. These things, which have the cause of their movements within themselves, some are said to move from themselves, others from themselves; and thus they divide so that they move from themselves, those that live indeed but are not animate, but animate things move from themselves, when fantasy, that is a certain will or incitement, is present to them, which provokes and incites them to move to something. Finally, even in certain animals there is such a fantasy, that is a will or sense, which provokes and incites them by a certain natural instinct to ordered and composed movements; as we see spiders doing, which are incited to the work of weaving in a very orderly way by a fantasy, that is by a certain will or zeal for weaving, without doubt a natural movement provoking the intention of this work, and yet the animal itself is not found to have any other sense than the natural zeal for weaving, just as the bee is said to make honeycombs and honey. But the rational animal, since it has within itself also these natural movements, has nevertheless more than the other animals also the power of reason, by which it can judge and discern about natural movements and reject and cast away some and approve and accept others, and the movements of man can be directed and governed to a probable life by the judgment of this reason. Whence it follows that, since the nature of this reason, which is in man, has within itself the power of distinguishing good and evil, and when it has distinguished, there is also in it the faculty of choosing what it has approved, and in choosing what is good it is praiseworthy, in following what is base or evil it is justly culpable. It is not to be hidden from us, that in some mute animals a more ordered movement is found than in other animals, as in clever dogs or war horses, so that they seem to be moved by a certain rational sense; but this is to be believed to happen not so much by reason as by a certain incitement and natural movement, which is more abundantly given for such uses. But as we began to say, since the rational animal is such, certain things can happen to us from outside and occur, either to sight or to hearing or to other senses, which provoke and incite us to good or contrary movements; which, since they happen from outside, are not in our power to prevent from happening or occurring: but to judge and approve how we ought to use these things that happen, is the work of no other thing than the reason that is in us, that is our judgment; by the judgment of which reason we use the incitements that happen from outside to whatever the reason itself has approved, and we govern our natural movements by its nod either to good or to contrary things. If indeed someone says that the things that happen from outside and provoke our movements are such that it is not possible to resist them, whether they incite us to good or to evil: let him turn his mind to himself for a little while and more diligently examine his own movements, and he will not find, when the allurements of some desire strike him, that anything is done before the assent of his mind is accommodated and the nod of his mind indulges the wicked suggestion; so that even in the tribunals of our heart, as it were, with the judge resident, an assertion seems to be made from both sides, so that a sentence about the judgment of reason may be pronounced after the causes have been set forth. For not, as I say by way of example, to him who has decided to live continently and chastely and to abstain from all feminine contagion, if perhaps a woman appears who provokes and incites him to do something against his purpose, is the woman a perfect and absolute cause or necessity for him to commit a sin, since he can indeed restrain the incitements of lust and coerce the delights of the alluring pleasure with the more austere precepts of virtue, so that the firmness and constancy of his purpose may persevere with all sense of luxury fled. Finally, if such incitements have come upon more erudite men and those strengthened in divine institutions, they, being mindful of themselves, immediately recall to memory what they have meditated upon and in which they have been instructed, and, fortifying themselves with the supports of a more holy doctrine, they reject and repel every allurement of incitement and drive away the contrary desires with the objection of the reason innate to them.

pass_b_english: We hold that certain teachings about God's promises must be grasped when we turn our understanding toward the contemplation of that endless, eternal age of praise, fixing our gaze on its indescribable joy and blessedness.

Yet because the Church's preaching also includes faith in the future judgment of God — a judgment whose certainty stirs people and urges them to live well and blessedly and to flee every kind of sin — it is plainly shown that it lies within our power to commit ourselves either to a praiseworthy life or a blameworthy one. For this reason I consider it necessary to say something, too, about the freedom of our will, since this question is being debated by very many people, and not without dignity.

So that we may more easily understand what freedom of will is, we must ask what the very nature of will and choice desires. Among all things that are moved, some carry the causes of their motion within themselves, while others receive them from outside. For example, everything without life — stones, wood, and whatever consists solely in the disposition of its matter or bodies — is moved only from without. We may set aside for now the question whether the motion of corruption, when bodies dissolve, counts as motion at all, because it does not serve our present purpose.

Other things, however, possess the cause of movement within themselves: animals, trees, and everything that subsists either through natural life or through a soul. Some have thought that even veins of metal, and perhaps the motion of fire and the sources of water, belong in this class. Among these self-moved things, some are said to move from themselves, others from themselves; thus they distinguish those that move from themselves because they live but are not animate, from animate things that move from themselves when fantasy — that is, a certain will or impulse — is present, provoking and urging them to move toward something.

Indeed, even in certain animals there is such a fantasy, a will or sense, which by a natural instinct stirs and incites them to ordered and composite movements. We see this in spiders, which are roused to the work of weaving in a remarkably orderly way by a fantasy, that is, by a certain will or zeal for weaving, a natural movement that prompts the intention of this work; yet the animal itself is found to possess no other sense than this natural zeal for weaving, just as the bee is said to fashion honeycombs and honey.

The rational animal, since it also has these natural movements within itself, nevertheless possesses something more than the other animals: the power of reason, by which it can judge and discern among natural movements, rejecting and casting away some, approving and accepting others, so that human movements may be directed and governed toward a worthy life by the judgment of this reason. It follows that, because the nature of this reason in man has within itself the power to distinguish good and evil, and once it has distinguished, there is also in it the faculty of choosing what it has approved. In choosing what is good it is praiseworthy; in following what is base or evil it is justly blameworthy.

We must not overlook the fact that in some mute animals a more ordered movement is found than in others — as in clever dogs or war horses — so that they appear to be moved by a kind of rational sense. But this is to be believed to happen not so much by reason as by a certain impulse and natural movement, more abundantly granted for such uses.

But to return to our starting point: since the rational animal is so constituted, certain things can befall us from outside and occur — whether to sight, hearing, or other senses — which provoke and incite us to good or contrary movements. Because these things happen from outside, it is not in our power to prevent them from happening or occurring. But to judge and determine how we ought to use these things that befall us is the work of nothing other than the reason that is in us, that is, our own judgment. By the judgment of this reason we employ the external incitements toward whatever reason itself has approved, and we govern our natural movements by its nod either toward good or toward contrary things.

If someone should claim that the external occurrences which provoke our movements are such that it is impossible to resist them, whether they incite us to good or to evil: let him turn his mind to himself for a little while and examine his own movements more closely. He will find that when the allurements of some desire strike him, nothing is done before the assent of his mind is given and the nod of his mind yields to the wicked suggestion — so that even in the tribunals of our heart, as it were, with the judge presiding, an argument seems to be made from both sides, that a sentence about the judgment of reason may be pronounced after the causes have been laid out.

For, to take an example, a man who has decided to live continently and chastely and to keep himself from all sexual contact is not forced into sin simply because a woman appears who provokes and entices him to act against his purpose. She is not a perfect and absolute cause or necessity of transgression for him, since he can certainly remember his resolve, restrain the incitements of lust, and curb the delights of the alluring pleasure with the stricter precepts of virtue, so that the firmness and constancy of his purpose may endure with every sense of luxury banished.

Finally, when such incitements come upon more learned men and those strengthened in divine institutions, they, mindful of themselves, immediately recall to memory what they have meditated on and been taught, and, fortifying themselves with the supports of a holier doctrine, they reject and repel every allurement of incitement and drive away contrary desires by the objection of the reason innate to them.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the nuances of agency (e.g., 'it is in our power to commit ourselves' for 'in nostra sit positum potestate') and the distinction between natural instinct and rational judgment. All clauses in the Latin source are accounted for in Pass B. Scripture citations (none present in this specific span) were not required.
